The Glenn-HT code is a general-purpose flow solver designed for simulations of flows in complicated geometries, based on the TRAF3D code.
The code employs the full compressible Navier-Stokes equations and uses a multi-stage Runge-Kutta scheme to march in pseudo time.
Convergence acceleration techniques used include local time stepping, implicit residual smoothing, and multigrid methods.
The k-ω turbulence model developed by Wilcox is used in the code, as it does not require the computation of the dimensionless wall distance y+.

The code has been used to simulate flow and heat transfer in a variety of geometries, including rectangular ducts with 180-degree turns, straight channels with ribs and bleed holes, and rotating channels with ribs and 180-degree turns.
The Method of Weakest Descent (MWD) is an automatic block merging algorithm that aims to produce the minimum number of blocks for a multi-block grid system.
Tests have shown that the MWD can typically produce a near-optimal number of blocks, with the probability of realizing the actual minimum increasing with repeated applications.
Structured multi-block grids require less memory and can take full advantage of convergence acceleration schemes compared to unstructured grids.
The rotating reference frame formulation in the code allows the grid system for the rotating geometry to be stationary, leading to computational savings.

The code uses inlet conditions specifying total temperature and pressure, exit pressure conditions, and wall conditions enforcing no-slip, specified temperature or heat flux, and special treatments for the turbulence quantities near walls.
The discretization in the code is formally second-order accurate, and artificial dissipation is added to prevent odd-even decoupling.
The code has been used for many types of flow fields including turbine blades, tip clearance flows, film cooling holes, and coolant channels.
The low-Reynolds number k-ω turbulence model used in the code has been shown to perform well in predicting heat transfer from flat plates and turbine blades.
The multi-block grid generation approach allows for accurate modeling of the complicated coolant passage geometries, which is essential for predicting heat transfer.
The convergence acceleration techniques employed in the code, such as local time stepping and multigrid, are crucial for enabling efficient simulations of these complex flow fields.
